title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 1
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: The Heat Island Beneath Our Feet
passages.text:
A. Cities are consistently warmer than the countryside surrounding them, a difference first described in London in 1818 and now measured in almost every urban area on earth. The gap is largest on still, clear nights and can exceed several degrees. What is less widely understood is that the effect is not primarily caused by waste heat from vehicles and buildings, though these contribute. It is caused chiefly by what cities are made of.

B. Construction materials are the dominant factor. Brick, concrete and asphalt have a far greater capacity to absorb and store solar energy than vegetation or soil, and they release it slowly through the night. A rural field cools rapidly after sunset because the water in its soil and plants has already carried much of the day's energy away through evaporation. A paved street has no such mechanism. It simply radiates the heat it accumulated, long after the sun has gone.

C. Geometry compounds the problem in ways that are easy to overlook. A narrow street between tall buildings forms what climatologists call an urban canyon. Radiation that would escape to the sky from an open field instead strikes a wall, reflects to the opposite wall, and is partially absorbed at each encounter. The taller the buildings relative to the width of the street, the more of the sky is hidden and the less efficiently heat escapes. Two districts with identical materials can therefore differ measurably in temperature purely because of how they are laid out.

D. The removal of vegetation matters for a reason that is frequently misstated. Trees are commonly described as cooling cities by providing shade, and they do. But the larger effect is evaporative: a mature tree moves substantial quantities of water from soil to atmosphere, and that transformation consumes energy which would otherwise raise air temperature. Shade without transpiration — an awning, for instance — delivers only part of the benefit.

E. The consequences are not distributed evenly, and this is where the science meets policy. Within a single city, temperature differences of several degrees are routinely recorded between neighbourhoods, and the hottest are consistently those with the least tree canopy, the most paved surface and the highest housing density. These are, in most cities studied, also the poorest. During heatwaves, the resulting excess mortality is concentrated in precisely those areas, among residents least able to afford cooling.

F. Remedies are well understood and unevenly applied. Increasing canopy cover, replacing dark impermeable surfaces with lighter or porous ones, and requiring reflective roofing all produce measurable reductions. What limits their adoption is rarely doubt about whether they work. It is that the cost falls on a developer or a municipal budget in one year while the benefit accrues to residents over decades — a mismatch of timing that no amount of further evidence resolves.

passages.title: The Invention of Standard Time
passages.text:
For most of human history, time was local. Noon was the moment the sun stood highest, and since that moment arrives later as one travels west, every town kept a clock that differed slightly from its neighbours. A traveller moving across a country adjusted continually, and nobody was inconvenienced, because nobody moved fast enough for the difference to matter.

The railway ended this arrangement. A train travelling at speed crossed several local times in a single journey, and a timetable expressed in local time became unusable. Worse, it became dangerous: on a single-track line, two trains running to timetables that disagreed by minutes could occupy the same section simultaneously. British railway companies adopted a single standard — the time kept at Greenwich — from the 1840s, decades before the state did. For a period, many towns displayed two times, and some public clocks were fitted with a second minute hand to show both.

Resistance was substantial and is often caricatured as mere conservatism. It was more considered than that. Local time was genuinely astronomical, tied to the sun's actual position; standard time was a convention imposed from elsewhere, and adopting it meant accepting that the clock no longer described the sky above one's own town. Several municipalities refused for years. Legal disputes turned on which time a contract referred to, and courts were obliged to rule on whether "noon" meant the local or the standard variety.

International coordination followed the same logic at a larger scale, and for the same reason: not scientific consensus but practical necessity in transport and telegraphy. The system of hourly zones agreed at an international conference in 1884 was not a discovery. It was a negotiated settlement, and the negotiation was largely about which meridian would serve as the origin — a question with no astronomical answer, decided by the weight of existing shipping charts.

What the episode illustrates is a pattern that recurs whenever a shared standard is established. The technical merits of the competing options were similar and were not what settled the matter; incumbency did. And once adopted, the standard became invisible: within a generation, few people experienced standard time as a convention at all, and the sense that noon is a fact about clocks rather than about the sun had become so ordinary that its recent origin was forgotten.

passages.title: What Sleep Research Has Revised
passages.text:
Sleep was long treated as a passive state — the absence of wakefulness, a period in which little of interest occurred. The development of electroencephalography in the twentieth century made it possible to record electrical activity during sleep, and the recordings showed something unexpected: sleep is not uniform, and the brain during certain phases is as active as during waking.

The identification of rapid eye movement sleep in the 1950s established the modern framework. Sleep proceeds in cycles of roughly ninety minutes, moving through progressively deeper non-REM stages before returning toward REM. The proportions shift across the night, with deep sleep concentrated early and REM periods lengthening toward morning. This structure explains a familiar observation: waking after a full night feels different from waking after four hours, not merely because of duration but because the composition of the sleep obtained differs.

Function has proved harder to establish than structure, and several confident accounts have been revised. The proposal that sleep exists primarily for energy conservation is now considered insufficient, since the metabolic saving is modest. A more durable finding concerns memory: material learned before sleep is retained better than material learned before an equivalent period of waking, and the effect is specific to certain sleep stages rather than to sleep generally. Whether this constitutes active consolidation or the mere absence of interference remains debated, and the distinction matters, since the two accounts predict different things about what an intervention could improve.

Deprivation studies have produced the most consistent results. Performance on tasks requiring sustained attention degrades rapidly and measurably, while performance on brief, engaging tasks degrades far less — which explains why sleep-deprived people frequently and sincerely report feeling fine. Self-assessment of impairment is unreliable in a specific direction: it underestimates, and the underestimation grows as deprivation continues.

A finding that has resisted popularisation concerns individual variation. The widely quoted eight-hour figure is a population average concealing substantial spread, and a small proportion of people function normally on considerably less. This has been distorted into the belief that anyone can adapt to short sleep, which the evidence does not support: the variation appears to be largely constitutional rather than trainable, and those who believe they have adapted usually show measurable impairment they cannot detect.

Timing is now understood to matter independently of duration. The circadian system regulates when sleep occurs efficiently, and sleeping against it — as shift workers must — produces poorer quality sleep of the same length. This has moved the field's attention from how much people sleep toward when, and toward the observation that a society organised around fixed early start times imposes a systematic cost on the substantial minority whose internal timing runs late.
